indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.content_standard: B5.4.2.1 Describe the likelihood of a single outcome occurring using words such as impossible, possible, and certain
indicator.objective: Design and conduct an experiment in which the likelihood of a single outcome occurring is impossible, possible (likely or unlikely), certain.

skills.description: Design an experiment with a specified likelihood (e.g., bag of red, green, pink bottle tops).
Conduct the experiment and record outcomes.

spec.difficultyPlan: 20 questions: 5 at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Designing an experiment that does not match the intended likelihood.

questions.stem: Which bag design makes picking a red ball impossible?
options: A bag with only blue balls
A bag with red and blue balls
A bag with only red balls
A bag with red, blue, and green balls
hints: Impossible means no red balls at all.
questions.explanation: A bag with only blue balls has no red balls, so picking red is impossible.
questions.misconception: Choosing a bag with some red balls.

questions.stem: Which bag design makes picking a red ball certain?
options: A bag with only red balls
A bag with red and blue balls
A bag with only blue balls
A bag with red and green balls
hints: Certain means every ball is red.
questions.explanation: A bag with only red balls makes picking red certain.
questions.misconception: Choosing a bag with mostly red.

questions.stem: To design an experiment where picking a blue bottle top is possible but unlikely, which bag should you use?
options: 1 blue and 19 red
10 blue and 10 red
20 blue
0 blue and 20 red
hints: Unlikely means few blue compared to red.
questions.explanation: 1 blue and 19 red makes blue possible but unlikely.

questions.stem: Conduct an experiment: Put 5 red counters and 5 blue counters in a bag. Pick one counter 10 times, replacing it each time. Record the colours.
hints: Replace the counter after each pick.
Make a tally for red and blue.
questions.explanation: The learner should record outcomes in a tally chart.

criteria.description: Picks 10 times and replaces each time.

questions.stem: Describe how to set up a bag so that picking a green ball is impossible.
hints: Use no green balls.
questions.explanation: Put only balls that are not green, for example only red and blue balls.

criteria.description: States no green balls in the bag.

questions.stem: Which experiment has a certain outcome?
options: Picking a red ball from a bag of only red balls
Picking a red ball from a bag of red and blue balls
Rolling a 6 on a die
Tossing a coin and getting tails
hints: Certain means it must happen.
questions.explanation: Picking from a bag of only red balls is certain.
questions.misconception: Choosing rolling a 6 because it is one outcome.

questions.stem: Design a simple experiment where the likelihood of picking a red bottle top is likely.
hints: Use more red than other colours.
questions.explanation: For example, put 8 red and 2 blue bottle tops in a bag. Picking red is likely.

criteria.description: Uses more red than other colours.

questions.stem: Conduct an experiment with a coin: Toss a coin 20 times and record heads and tails.
hints: Make a tally chart for heads and tails.

questions.stem: A bag has 12 red and 2 green balls. Picking a green ball is:
options: Impossible
Possible but unlikely
Certain
Likely
hints: There are few green balls.

questions.stem: Explain how to record outcomes in a probability experiment.
hints: Use tallies or a table.
questions.explanation: Make a table or tally chart for each possible outcome. Put a mark each time the outcome occurs.
questions.misconception: Trying to remember outcomes without recording.

questions.stem: Design an experiment where landing on blue is impossible using a spinner with 4 equal sectors.
hints: Do not use blue on the spinner.
questions.explanation: Use colours such as red, green, yellow, and orange, with no blue sector.

questions.stem: Conduct a spinner experiment: Spin a 4-sector spinner 16 times and record where it lands.
hints: Use a tally chart for each sector.

questions.stem: A pupil wants an experiment where picking a red counter is possible but unlikely. Describe a bag they could use.
hints: Use few red counters compared to other colours.
questions.explanation: For example, 1 red and 15 blue counters.

questions.stem: Explain why it is important to replace the counter after each pick in a bag experiment.
hints: Replacing keeps the probabilities the same.
questions.explanation: Replacing keeps the number of each colour the same for every pick, so the likelihood does not change.

criteria.description: States it keeps probabilities the same.

questions.stem: Design an experiment where picking a green ball is certain.
hints: All balls must be green.
questions.explanation: Put only green balls in the bag.

questions.stem: Conduct an experiment: Roll a die 30 times. Record how many times each number appears.
hints: Use a tally chart for 1 to 6.

questions.stem: Explain why the same experiment can give different results when repeated.
hints: Random outcomes vary.
questions.explanation: Random outcomes can vary from trial to trial, so repeated experiments may not give exactly the same results.
questions.misconception: Thinking results must always match exactly.

questions.stem: Design an experiment with a bag of counters to show an impossible, a possible, and a certain outcome. Describe the bag and the three outcomes.
hints: Use colours with different quantities.
questions.explanation: For example, a bag with 10 red and 1 blue: impossible = picking green; possible = picking blue; certain = picking red or blue.

criteria.description: Gives one outcome of each type.

questions.misconception: Not matching outcomes to bag contents.

questions.stem: A pupil conducts 50 coin tosses and records 30 heads and 20 tails. Explain what these results show.
hints: Compare to expected 25 heads and 25 tails.
questions.explanation: The results are close to expected but not exactly equal. Random variation explains the difference.
questions.misconception: Thinking the coin is unfair because not exactly 25.
